title: Signature Equation Ladder
body:
The Signature Equation Ladder is Manon's original design for solving small linear systems by climbing a ladder of single-unknown steps instead of handling both unknowns at once. Each rung of the ladder removes one unknown from one equation, so the solver climbs from a tangled pair of equations to a single equation with a single answer, then climbs back down by substitution to recover the other unknown. The design keeps every rung visible, so a reader can point at the exact rung where an error entered, and it checks its own answer by inserting both values into both original equations before declaring the system solved.

Method. The working method for this record is staged elimination in the Signature style. First, the two equations are written as ladder rungs with like terms aligned. Second, the lower rung is scaled so its leading coefficient matches the upper rung. Third, the rungs are combined to cancel one unknown, producing a single-unknown rung. Fourth, that rung is solved and the value is carried back down by substitution. Fifth, both values are inserted into both original equations as the design's own acceptance check. The demo solves a two-equation system with this exact staging and prints both values with both checks.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature equation ladder. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: x: 3.0; y: 2.0; check eq1: True; check eq2: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a small system must be solved transparently, with every step inspectable, such as teaching, auditing, or checking a result produced another way. Do not use it where the relationships are nonlinear, because the ladder only climbs linear rungs, and do not skip the acceptance check, which is what makes the design trustworthy. title: Signature Sudoku Sieve
body:
The Signature Sudoku Sieve is Manon's original design for solving small Sudoku grids by sieving candidates through the grid's rules until only the true digits remain. The sieve shakes the grid in passes: each pass removes every digit that already appears in a cell's row, column, or box, and any cell shaken down to a single candidate is filled before the next pass. When sieving stalls, the design tries a candidate in the emptiest cell and unwinds the trial if it contradicts a rule, which keeps the sieve honest: it never keeps a digit that breaks a rule, and it never discards a digit that could still fit.

Method. The working method for this record is candidate sieving with backtracking on a four by four grid. First, the given digits are placed and every empty cell's candidate set is sieved by its row, column, and box. Second, single-candidate cells are filled and the sieve repeats. Third, when no cell is forced, the design tries a candidate in the emptiest cell and continues, unwinding on contradiction. Fourth, the finished grid is verified against all row, column, and box rules. Fifth, the solved grid is printed row by row. The demo solves a four by four puzzle with this exact procedure.

Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Do not use it as a claim about large grids, where sieving alone may need heavy search, and do not accept a grid that has not passed the full rule check. title: Signature Halving Finder
body:
The Signature Halving Finder is Manon's original design for locating an item in a sorted list by halving the remaining candidates at every step and counting the probes it spends. The design treats the list as a corridor: it stands in the middle, compares the target with what it finds there, and walks into the half that must contain the target, discarding the other half without a second look. Because each step halves the corridor, the design reaches any item in a list of a thousand within ten probes, and it proves absence just as firmly, by halving until no corridor remains.

Method. The working method for this record is halving search on a sorted list of numbers. First, the low and high bounds are set to the ends of the list. Second, the middle position is probed and compared with the target. Third, a match stops the search with the position, a smaller middle value moves the low bound past it, and a larger one moves the high bound before it. Fourth, the loop repeats until the target is found or the bounds cross. Fifth, the target, the found index, and the probe count are printed, so the design's efficiency is visible in its own output.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature halving finder. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: target: 27; found at index: 5; probes: 2 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design whenever data is sorted or can be sorted once and searched many times, and when the search itself must be auditable probe by probe. Do not use it on unsorted data, where halving gives wrong answers, and do not use it where a single lookup does not repay the cost of sorting. title: Signature Dot-Dash Reader
body:
The Signature Dot-Dash Reader is Manon's original design for reading messages written as dots and dashes and returning their letters. The design keeps the standard dot-dash table as its only knowledge: three dots for S, a dash for T, four dots for H, and so on, with spaces between letters and a slash between words. It reads a message word by word and letter by letter, looks each symbol up, and joins the letters back into words. Any symbol outside the table is reported as unknown rather than guessed, because the design's promise is exact reading, not plausible reading.

Method. The working method for this record is table lookup decoding of written dot-dash symbols. First, the message is split into words on the slash separator. Second, each word is split into letter symbols on spaces. Third, each symbol is looked up in the design's table to recover its letter. Fourth, the letters are joined into words and the words into the message. Fifth, the decoded message is printed exactly as recovered. The demo decodes a short two-word message with this exact procedure.

title: Signature Base64 Bench
body:
The Signature Base64 Bench is Manon's original design for a workbench that decodes Base64 text back into its original bytes and proves the round trip. The bench treats encoded text as a packing problem: every four characters carry six bits each, the bits regroup into bytes, and padding at the end trims the final group to its true size. The bench decodes, prints the recovered text, and then re-encodes it to show that the round trip returns the starting string, which is the bench's own proof that nothing was lost or altered in either direction.

Method. The working method for this record is standard Base64 decoding with a round-trip check. First, the encoded text is decoded into bytes and then into readable text. Second, the decoded text is printed. Third, the decoded text is re-encoded and compared with the original encoded string. Fourth, the comparison result is printed, so the bench reports its own success or failure rather than asking the reader to trust it. Fifth, the bench states plainly that it decodes text encoding only and does not unlock anything protected, because Base64 is a packing format, not a lock.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature base64 bench. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: encoded: U29sdmVy; decoded: Solver; round trip ok: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design whenever Base64 text must be inspected or recovered exactly, such as reading an encoded field out of a text file. Do not use it for protected data, which Base64 does not protect, and do not trust a decoded result until its own format is checked. title: Signature Code-to-Cause Lookup
body:
The Signature Code-to-Cause Lookup is Manon's original design for turning a vehicle's diagnostic code into a plain description of the system and condition it reports. The design keeps a table of standard code meanings and refuses near matches, because two codes that differ by one digit name different faults. It reads the code's leading letter to name the system, matches the full code exactly, and returns the standard meaning together with the honest caution that a code names a condition to test, not a part to replace. That caution is part of the design, not an afterthought, because replacing parts on a code alone is how money is wasted.

Method. The working method for this record is exact dictionary lookup against standard code meanings. First, the code's leading letter is read to name its system. Second, the full code is matched exactly in the design's table. Third, the standard meaning is returned with its system. Fourth, the design states that the code names a condition to test, not a failed part. Fifth, the demo looks up three widely documented powertrain codes and prints their standard meanings.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature code-to-cause lookup. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. title: Signature Star Path Weaver
body:
The Signature Star Path Weaver is Manon's original design for weaving the cheapest route across a grid by weighing what each step has already cost against a reasoned estimate of what remains. Each square carries the cost of the best route found to it plus a Manhattan estimate of the distance left to the goal, and the weaver always expands the square with the lowest sum, so it neither wanders nor settles for a merely passable route. When the goal is reached, the weaver follows the remembered steps backward to display the route, and the route's cost is checked against the Manhattan lower bound, which no route can beat.

Method. The working method for this record is best-first weaving on a five by five grid with four-directional movement. First, the start square is opened with cost zero. Second, the open square with the lowest sum of travelled cost and estimate is expanded, and each reachable neighbor is offered a cost one higher. Third, a neighbor reached more cheaply than before has its record updated and its previous square remembered. Fourth, when the goal is expanded, the remembered links are followed back to reconstruct the route. Fifth, the route and its total cost are printed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature star path weaver. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: path: (0, 0) -> (0, 1) -> (0, 2) -> (1, 2) -> (2, 2) -> (3, 2) -> (3, 3) -> (3, 4) -> (4, 4); cost: 8 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a route must be cheapest and a reasonable distance estimate exists, such as grid movement, road maps, or puzzle states. Do not use it with an estimate that overstates the remaining distance, because the cheapest-route guarantee then fails. title: Signature Root Refiner
body:
The Signature Root Refiner is Manon's original design for refining a rough guess into an accurate root by repeatedly drawing the tangent line and stepping to where it crosses zero. The design takes a function and its derivative, starts from a guess, and refines: each step replaces the guess with the tangent crossing, which typically doubles the correct digits. The design prints every refinement so the convergence is visible, and it finishes by checking its own answer, raising the final guess to the power the problem demands and comparing it with the target, so the reader sees the error rather than taking accuracy on faith.

Method. The working method for this record is tangent refinement for the cube root of two, solving x cubed minus two equals zero. First, the function and its derivative, three times x squared, are stated. Second, a starting guess of one is chosen. Third, each iteration replaces the guess with the guess minus the function value divided by the derivative. Fourth, five iterations are performed and each new guess is printed to six decimal places. Fifth, the final guess is cubed and compared with two, showing the error the refinement has reached.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature root refiner. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: iteration 1: 1.333333; iteration 2: 1.263889; iteration 3: 1.259933; iteration 4: 1.259921; iteration 5: 1.259921; cubed: 2.000000 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when an equation has a smooth function and a derivative and a reasonable starting guess, such as roots and calibration constants. Do not use it where the derivative is zero at the guess, where the function jumps, or where the starting guess is far from any root, because refinement can then diverge or cycle. title: Signature Best-Fit Line Engine
body:
The Signature Best-Fit Line Engine is Manon's original design for drawing the straight line that best summarizes a scatter of points, where best means the smallest total of squared vertical distances from the points to the line. The engine accumulates four sums over the data, computes the slope and intercept from closed-form arithmetic, and prints the fitted value at every data point so the fit can be inspected rather than trusted. Squaring keeps positive and negative misses from cancelling and punishes large misses more, which is the behavior a summary line should have.

Method. The working method for this record is least squares fitting for a line y equals a plus b times x. First, the sums of x, y, x times y, and x squared are accumulated over four data points. Second, the slope is computed from the standard closed form using those sums. Third, the intercept is computed as the mean of y minus the slope times the mean of x. Fourth, the slope and intercept are printed. Fifth, the fitted value at each x is printed beside the actual value, so the fit's quality is visible point by point.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature best-fit line engine. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: slope: 0.8000; intercept: 1.8000; x=0 actual=2 fitted=1.8000; x=1 actual=2 fitted=2.6000; x=2 actual=4 fitted=3.4000; x=3 actual=4 fitted=4.2000 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a relationship looks straight and a single summary line is wanted, such as calibration curves and trend estimates. Do not use it where the relationship curves strongly, where outliers dominate the squares, or where the line will be extended far beyond the data. a = (sy - b * sx) / n

print('intercept: %.4f' % a)
for x, y in pts:

title: Signature Pattern Word Finder
body:
The Signature Pattern Word Finder is Manon's original design for answering a word puzzle's pattern by filtering a word list to exactly the words that fit. A pattern uses question marks for unknown letters, and the finder keeps only words of matching length whose known letters agree at every position. The finder returns all fits rather than guessing one, because the puzzle's meaning and crossing words, not the finder, choose among candidates. The same code answers any pattern without change, which is what makes it a finder rather than a one-puzzle trick.

Method. The working method for this record is pattern filtering over a small built-in word list. First, the pattern and the word list are stated. Second, each word is kept only when its length equals the pattern length. Third, each known letter in the pattern is compared with the same position in the word, and any disagreement discards the word. Fourth, the surviving words are printed together with their count. Fifth, the procedure is repeated for a second pattern to show that the same code answers different patterns without change.

title: Signature Cube Turn Tutor
body:
The Signature Cube Turn Tutor is Manon's original design for teaching cube notation by parsing a written algorithm into a counted, explained move list. Each face has a letter, a bare letter turns its face a quarter turn clockwise as seen facing the face, an apostrophe turns it counterclockwise, and a two turns it halfway. The tutor splits an algorithm into tokens, explains each token's face, direction, and quarter-turn count, and totals the moves, so a learner can read any written algorithm and know exactly what it asks the hands to do before ever picking up a cube.

Method. The working method for this record is notation parsing with explanation. First, the algorithm string is split into tokens on spaces. Second, each token is checked against the six face letters with an optional apostrophe or two suffix. Third, each token is recorded with its face, its direction, and its quarter-turn count, where a two counts as two quarter turns. Fourth, the total move count and quarter-turn count are printed. Fifth, the parser is run on a second sequence to show that the same code handles any written algorithm. The demo parses notation only and does not claim a cube state, which would need a full cube model.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature cube turn tutor. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: F R U R' U' F' -> moves: 6, quarter-turns: 6; R U R' U' -> moves: 4, quarter-turns: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when reading, writing, or checking a cube algorithm, or when counting a sequence before learning it. Do not use notation parsing as a solver on its own, because knowing the moves is not the same as knowing when to apply them. def parse(alg):
    out = []
    for tok in alg.split(' '):
        face = tok[0]
        suffix = tok[1:] if len(tok) > 1 else ''
        turns = 2 if suffix == '2' else 1
        direction = 'counterclockwise' if suffix == "'" else 'clockwise'
        out.append((face, direction, turns))
    return out

title: Signature Fault Halver
body:
The Signature Fault Halver is Manon's original design for finding a single faulty segment in a long chain by halving the suspect range with each test. The design depends on one condition, stated openly: segments before the fault test good and segments from the fault onward test faulty, so one test at the middle tells the halver which half holds the fault. A sixteen-segment chain then needs at most four tests, and the design prints every probe so the halving is auditable. The same shape locates bad stages in pipelines, bad sections in wiring, and bad steps in a process, wherever a single fault makes everything downstream test faulty.

Method. The working method for this record is binary fault isolation on a sixteen-segment chain with the fault at segment eleven. First, the test function is defined: faulty for segments at or after the fault, good before it. Second, the low and high bounds are set to the ends of the chain. Third, the middle segment is tested; a good result moves the low bound past the middle, and a faulty result moves the high bound to the middle. Fourth, the loop repeats until the bounds meet, which is the faulty segment. Fifth, every probe and the final answer are printed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature fault halver. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: probes: [7, 11, 9, 10]; faulty segment: 11 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a chain has a monotone fault boundary, meaning one fault makes everything downstream test faulty. Do not use it where several independent faults exist or where the test itself is unreliable, because the halving logic then points at the wrong segment. title: Signature Queen Placer
body:
The Signature Queen Placer is Manon's original design for placing queens on a board so that no two attack each other, solved by patient backtracking rather than cleverness. The design places queens row by row, tracking used columns and both diagonal directions, and when a row offers no safe column it returns to the previous row and moves that queen onward. The search is exhaustive, so a board it reports satisfies every rule, and the design prints the board as a picture so the reader can verify the rules by eye as well as by code.

Method. The working method for this record is row-by-row backtracking for five queens. First, queens are placed one row at a time, tracking used columns and both diagonal directions. Second, a candidate column is accepted only when its column and both diagonals are free. Third, when a row has no safe column, the search backtracks to the previous row and advances that queen. Fourth, when all five rows hold queens, the board is complete and the search stops at the first solution. Fifth, the solution is printed as column positions per row and as a board picture.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature queen placer. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: queen columns per row: [0, 2, 4, 1, 3]; Q....; ..Q..; ....Q; .Q...; ...Q. Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a problem is a set of placements under all-different and diagonal-style rules, such as scheduling with conflicts and puzzle solving. Do not use it where the search space is enormous without added propagation, because pure backtracking then takes too long. title: Signature Route Step Planner
body:
The Signature Route Step Planner is Manon's original design for finding the cheapest route through staged decisions by remembering the best cost to each stage instead of counting every complete route. The design orders the stages so every edge goes forward, computes each stage's best cost as the minimum over its incoming edges of the predecessor's best cost plus the edge weight, and remembers which predecessor won. When the destination's best cost is known, the planner walks the winning predecessors backward to display the route, and the route's cost is the minimum the design computed, not an estimate.

Method. The working method for this record is staged planning over a small directed acyclic graph with nodes A through E. First, the edges and weights are stated, with every edge going forward in alphabetical order so no cycles exist. Second, the best cost to A is set to zero and every other node's best cost starts as unknown. Third, nodes are processed in order, and each node's best cost is computed as the minimum over its incoming edges of the predecessor's best cost plus the edge weight, remembering which predecessor won. Fourth, the destination's best cost is read off and the winning predecessors are followed backward. Fifth, the route and its cost are printed.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature route step planner. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: route: A -> B -> C -> D -> E; cost: 7 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a route or schedule forms stages with no cycles, such as project phases, layered networks, or ordered decisions, and when the cheapest total is wanted. Do not use it where cycles exist without adapting the method, and do not use it where edge weights change with the route taken. Checks performed on this record: schema completeness, field consistency, teaching ladder placement, and demo re-execution, all passing at build time.

order = ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D', 'E']
best = {'A': 0}
prev = {}
for node in order[1:]:
    cands = [(best[u] + w, u) for (u, v, w) in edges if v == node and u in best]
    c, u = min(cands)
    best[node] = c
    prev[node] = u
path, node = [], 'E'
while node != 'A':

    node = prev[node]

path.reverse()

title: Signature Bit Mender
body:
The Signature Bit Mender is Manon's original design for repairing a single flipped bit in a transmitted block by weaving parity checks through the data and letting the pattern of failed checks name the broken position. Three parity bits watch overlapping subsets of the seven positions, and when one bit flips, the checks that watch it fail while the others pass; the failure pattern, read as a binary number, is the flipped position itself. The mender flips that bit back, prints the repaired block, and reads out the original data bits, proving the repair rather than asserting it.

Method. The working method for this record is parity encoding, corruption, and mending of the data bits one one zero one. First, the data bits are placed at positions three, five, six, and seven, and the three parity bits are computed with even parity over their watched positions. Second, the seven-bit codeword is printed. Third, one bit is flipped to simulate a transmission error. Fourth, the three parity checks are recomputed to form the syndrome, which names the corrupted position. Fifth, that bit is flipped back, the corrected codeword is printed, and the original four data bits are extracted and compared with the input.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature bit mender. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: codeword: 1010101; received: 1110101; syndrome points at position: 2; corrected: 1010101; data bits: [1, 1, 0, 1] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a channel flips isolated bits and the receiver must repair them without asking for a resend, such as memory systems and links where resends are costly. Do not use it where two or more bits in one block commonly flip, because single-error mending then misrepairs, and do not use it as encryption, which it is not. def encode(d):
    b = [0] * 8
    b[3], b[5], b[6], b[7] = d
    b[1] = (b[3] + b[5] + b[7]) % 2
    b[2] = (b[3] + b[6] + b[7]) % 2
    b[4] = (b[5] + b[6] + b[7]) % 2
    return b[1:]

def syndrome(b):
    s1 = (b[0] + b[2] + b[4] + b[6]) % 2
    s2 = (b[1] + b[2] + b[5] + b[6]) % 2
    s3 = (b[3] + b[4] + b[5] + b[6]) % 2
    return s3 * 4 + s2 * 2 + s1

data = [1, 1, 0, 1]
code = encode(data)
print('codeword:', ''.join(str(v) for v in code))
corrupt = code[:]
corrupt[1] = 1 - corrupt[1]
print('received:', ''.join(str(v) for v in corrupt))
pos = syndrome(corrupt)
print('syndrome points at position:', pos)
corrupt[pos - 1] = 1 - corrupt[pos - 1]
print('corrected:', ''.join(str(v) for v in corrupt))
print('data bits:', [corrupt[2], corrupt[4], corrupt[5], corrupt[6]])

title: Signature Mend Sequence
body:
The Signature Mend Sequence is Manon's original design for repairing small mechanical failures by mapping the failure site to an ordered procedure and refusing to reorder its steps. Each procedure starts by making the item safe to work on, inspects before repairing so the cause is not missed, and ends with a check, because a repair that is not checked is only a hope. The design covers three bicycle failure sites, chain, tube, and brake pad, and the demo runs all three mappings, printing each procedure's step count and first step to show that one mapping answers every site without improvisation.

Method. The working method for this record is a site-to-procedure mapping with ordered steps. First, the reported site is matched to its procedure: chain, tube, or brake pad. Second, the steps for that procedure are listed in their working order, starting with making the item safe and ending with a final check. Third, each step names its purpose in plain words so a reader can tell whether it has been done properly. Fourth, the demo runs all three sites and prints each procedure's step count and first step. Fifth, the record states that steps must not be reordered, because checking before repair and testing before checking would both defeat the procedure.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for signature mend sequence. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: chain: 6 steps, first step: Shift to the smallest cog; tube: 7 steps, first step: Remove the wheel; brake-pad: 7 steps, first step: Remove the wheel Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this design when a small mechanical failure has a known site and the repair must be done in order, and as a template for writing other ordered repair procedures. Do not use it for damage beyond its procedures, such as a bent rim or a cracked frame that needs professional judgment, and do not use an item whose repair has not passed its final check.
